title: Clonal Hematopoeisis of Indeterminate Potential and Risk of Autopsy-defined Sudden Cardiac Death
text:
Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) is an occult pre-cancerous proliferation of cells in
the blood that leads to an increase in cardiovascular disease and overall mortality. The association between
CHIP and sudden cardiac death (SCD) and the mechanism by which CHIP might contribute to SCD remain
unknown. We propose targeted sequencing for CHIP in blood and heart samples from our unique cohort of
autopsy-confirmed SCDs, and quantitative histologic and molecular phenotyping of heart tissue to determine
how CHIP contributes to vulnerable substrate for lethal arrhythmias underlying SCD.

title: Data Analysis and Coordination Core
text: Abstract The Data Analysis and Coordination Core (DACC) will provide critical infrastructure and expertise to support the MI- CARB Program’s eDorts to understand and prevent infections from antibiotic resistant pathogens and Clostridioides di+icile. The core will streamline data management, integrating complex clinical, microbiome, and multi-omics datasets while ensuring security, accessibility, and rigor. It will provide bioinformatics support for integrating microbial sequence data into analyses, biostatistical expertise for modeling, and advanced machine learning approaches to analyze high-dimensional data. Additionally, the DACC will oversee biospecimen tracking and management, ensuring proper linkage to patient metadata and facilitating data deposition in public repositories. By centralizing these key functions, the core will enhance the eDiciency, reproducibility, and impact of the MI-CARB research program, enabling the discovery of actionable microbial targets for further study.

title: Network and Systems Biology Scientific Core 3
text: SC3 PROJECT SUMMARY Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common arrhythmia and a major risk factor for cardiovascular mortality and stroke. Incidence of AF is further increasing due to the rise in obesity and age of the population, factors closely related to AF risk and progression. Despite significant advances in AF diagnosis and management, treatment and clinical outcomes remain poor and more than a decade has passed since the last AF drug discovery. The overall goal of this PPG application is to use genomic and transcriptomic findings to identify preventative and therapeutic strategies for AF and develop them towards clinical application. Our central hypothesis is that increasing our knowledge about molecular mechanisms involved in genetic, transcriptomic, metabolic and structural changes in the atria will allow us to pinpoint possible targets for safer and more effective therapeutic strategies. To help the projects advance towards these goals, the Network and Systems Biology Core (SC3) will be responsible for the processing, analysis, integration and network modeling of all RNA sequencing data, including bulk and single nuclei, proteomic, metabolomics, and functional assay data used and generated in the four projects. All Projects have proposed extensive use of RNA sequencing studies, making SC3 integral to their success. Functional assay data will be generated primarily in SC1 and SC2 under direction of the Projects and then sent to SC3 for analysis and integration with RNASeq. SC3 will work closely with the project leads and personnel to help interpret and visualize the results including those from traditional differential analyses as well as from more advanced network and systems biology approaches. SC3 has a unique blend of expertise and experience, combining personnel with RNA processing and modeling skills and those with a network and systems biology focus, which together with a rigorous and reproducible pipeline implementation will help enable the four projects in this PPG to fill knowledge gaps and make advances towards understanding and treating atrial fibrillation. SC3 will provide two major groups of services to the PPG organized around the type of data being analyzed. Aim 1 will focus on services for RNA sequencing data, including advanced network and systems biology approaches, while Aim 2 will focus on services for functional assay data as well as integrations with the RNA data.

title: Progesterone Receptor (PR) Signaling Cross Talk Drives ER+ Breast Cancer
text:
Many patients with hormone receptor-positive (ER+/PR+) breast cancer experience tumor recurrence, even after
successful initial treatment and often many years to decades later. Evidence supports the concept that ER+
breast cancer cells can enter a durable quiescent dormant state, evade ER-targeted therapies and later
reawaken to cause tumor recurrence and metastases. Herein, we seek to uncover new hormone receptor-driven
mechanisms of cell cycle regulation and tumor cell dormancy that may be targeted to eliminate dormant breast
cancer cells, prevent late recurrence, and improve healthy longevity for patients suffering from ER+ breast
cancer.

title: Role of the Long Non-Coding RNA TERRA in Regulating DNA Repair Pathways at Telomeres
text:
Repair of dysfunctional telomeres results in telomere–telomere fusions that initiate large-scale chromosomal
rearrangements and contribute to genome instability in aging and cancer. This project will define the molecular
mechanisms by which the long noncoding telomeric repeat-containing RNA (TERRA) drives telomere fusions
through the organization of DNA damage response factors into repair condensates to promote telomere mobility
and clustering. These studies will advance understanding of telomere biology and RNA-mediated DNA repair
and will provide mechanistic insight into genome instability underlying human disease.

title: Histology
text: Histology Core: Project Summary/Abstract Koch Institute Members use vertebrate model organisms as a key tool to study the role of known or putative cancer genes in development and tumorigenicity; investigate the mechanisms of tumor initiation, progression and metastasis; evaluate the role of stroma and immune responses in tumorigenesis; and assess the efficacy of drugs, nanomaterials and devices in therapeutic and diagnostic applications. Thus, it is essential that Center Members are able to correctly diagnose developmental and tumor phenotypes, evaluate the underlying molecular events, and accurately and quantitatively assess drug or vaccine delivery, localized tissue response, and overall therapeutic response. The Koch Institute Histology Core is a Shared Resource that provides state- of-the-art histological services to support these studies. This includes assistance and/or training in tissue sectioning, slide preparation, staining and analysis, and access to the consultative services of an internationally recognized Veterinary Pathologist, Dr. Roderick Bronson, for diagnosis of tumor and tissue phenotypes. During the current period, usage of the Histology Core increased from 67% to 77% of Center Members, and included investigators from all three Programs. In response to Center member needs, the Histology Core expanded services and instrumentation. This includes expanded offerings for immunohistochemistry and special stains, and investigator training for independent sectioning. The Core also acquired new digital slide scanning capabilities and quantification software, and made upgrades to existing key instrumentation. Thus, this Shared Resource is essential to the success of the Koch Institute mission. In the upcoming period, The Histology Core is committed to offering a wide range of state-of-the-art histological services to support the research programs of Center Members. Planned initiatives include: working with the Integrated Genomics & Bioinformatics Core to establish methodologies for mapping gene expression at the single cell level within tissues; developing expertise and providing guidance in use of automated AI-driven analysis packages (such as QuPath) for analysis of histological sections; evaluating instrumentation to determine community benefit for fluorescent digital slide scanning; and expanding histology training offerings to include more hands-on workshop opportunities. This shared Core is of exceptional value to the CCSG because Koch Institute Members account for 95% of the Core services usage. Notably, the requested CCSG budget for Year 49 is 6.8% less than the budget in the current period (Year 48).

title: Neuroimmune Control of Microbiota-Evoked Hyperinnervation and Pruritus
text:
Pruritus, or itch, is a complex condition with an unclear pathogenesis, involving interactions between immune
cells and unmyelinated C-fiber sensory neurons. Although sensory neuron hyperinnervation is a key feature in
the skin of pruritus patients, the mechanisms behind nerve overgrowth and its role in itch remain poorly
understood. This proposal aims to explore how microbiota-driven neuroimmune regulation influences
hyperinnervation and pruritus, with the ultimate goal of identifying novel therapeutic approaches for pruritus and
other inflammatory skin diseases.

title: "Charting cellular attraction-based interactome with Multivalent Adhesive Probe AFM (MAPA)"
text:
Changes in cell surface adhesion provide a sensitive indicator of cancer cell invasiveness.
However, the parameter of cell attractiveness is underutilized in cancer cell biology due to the
lack of robust methods offering both qualitative and quantitative measures. Here we propose to
develop a Multivalent Adhesive Probe Atomic force microscopy based method (MAPA) for
simultaneous quantitating the attraction of cancer cells and tissue samples and determining the
physicochemical mechanism behind the surface adhesiveness.

title: Inhibitory Control and Externalizing Behaviors in Youth at Risk for Huntington Disease
text:
Recent advances toward potential disease-modifying therapies in Huntington disease (HD)
present an urgent need to identify early, quantifiable markers of disease progression in youth
and young adults at risk for HD. The goals of this study are to characterize impulsive behaviors
as an early marker of HD and to examine the influence of genetic status, environmental
stressors, and inhibitory control as potential predictors of these behaviors. These results will
lead to better understanding and improved detection of the earliest symptoms of HD, which will
help to guide the development of new therapies for those at risk of developing this fatal disease.

title: BLR&D Research Career Scientist Award
text:
This research is highly relevant to the healthcare of veterans, who comprise an aging
population with elevated incidence of traumatic brain injury (TBI). Both age and TBI
increase the risk of AD, PD, and other neurodegenerative diseases. By seeking basic
principles that govern protein aggregation across many neuropathies, we hope to
gain insights and develop novel interventions (e.g., drugs) that apply to diverse
neurological pathologies including “orphan diseases” that are too rare or underfunded
to attract substantial research effort aimed at their prevention or cure.

title: Interdisciplinary Training in Systems & Biomolecular Data Science
text:
Biomedical research now requires the use of computational methods and systems models to (i) process the
large data current technologies generate, (ii) integrate different data types into a cohesive picture of the
biological processes that are studied, (iii) test hypotheses about how the biological processes function, and (iv)
generate new, testable hypotheses that further our biological understanding. Scientists that can develop and
use these computational methods and systems models require cross-disciplinary training in collaboration,
scientific rigor, and quantitative methods. The Systems & Biomolecular Data Sciences training program brings
together 12 degree-granting programs and 34 faculty mentors across the UVA Schools of Medicine,
Engineering, Data Science, and Arts & Sciences to prepare this next generation of transdisciplinary biomedical
scientists at the interface of quantitative biology, systems biology, machine learning, and informatics.

title: Investigating mechanisms underlying diabetes associated with exocrine pancreas diseases
text:
Type 3c diabetes mellitus (T3cD) accompanies exocrine pancreas diseases like chronic
pancreatitis (CP) and has distinct clinical features and greater prevalence than previously
appreciated, but the mechanisms underlying T3cD are poorly understood. From studies of islets
in living subjects with CP, we have identified molecular and functional changes in islet cells that
could promote prediabetes. In this proposal we aim to identify signaling and genetic
mechanisms underlying islet dysfunction in pre-T3cD development.

title: Addressing tumor heterogeneity in pediatric gliomas with precision adoptive T cell therapy
text:
Despite a multi-modal standard of care treatment approach including radiation therapy,
chemotherapy, and surgical resection, the outcome remains poor for pediatric high-grade gliomas
necessitating the development of new therapies. We have previously established an FDA IND-
approved personalized adoptive cellular therapy (ACT) platform utilizing total tumor RNA-pulsed
dendritic cells (DCs) to expand polyclonal tumor-specific T cells for the treatment of invasive and
refractory brain cancers. In this proposal, we will explore a superior approach utilizing the
identification and selective amplification of patients’ tumor-specific antigens and uniquely
identifying, sorting, and expanding responding tumor-specific T cells for use in ACT to improve
the eradication of invasive HGG before pursuing an early phase human clinical trial.

title: Secreted genetically encoded fluorescent biosensors for in vivo extracellular imaging
text:
Genetically encoded fluorescent biosensors are essential tools for investigating a wide range of biochemical
processes in living organisms. This proposal aims to develop secreted genetically encoded biosensors to enable
novel in vivo imaging applications including real-time characterization of extracellular matrix remodeling,
extracellular ion and oxygen dynamics, cell death pathways, and interstitial fluid flow. By combining our newly
developed biosensors with custom optical microscopes, we aim to substantially advance our understanding of
fundamental biological processes within the extracellular space.

title: The NINDS Human Cell and Data Repository (U24 renewal)
text:
iPSC are increasingly utilized in disease modeling, drug discovery, toxicological testing, and clinical
applications and the need for high quality, well characterized biomaterials is clear and pressing. The NHCDR,
Rutgers and SAMPLED will continue to serve the global scientific community by providing source cells, iPSC
and isogenic iPSC pairs from subjects with neurological disorders such as Parkinson’s disease, Alzheimer’s
disease, Huntington’s disease, Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis, Dystonia and Frontotemporal Degeneration.

title: Characterizing representational geometry and learning across primate visual streams
text:
The ventral stream of the visual system has long been known to contribute to aphasia or memory loss when
damaged, however it remains unclear how specific parts of the ventral stream contribute to these deficits. The
current study will separately characterize responses in the ventral stream, and computationally model different
sub-parts of the ventral stream, including the perirhinal (Pr) and parhippocamapal (Ph) subdivisions.
Understanding the ventral visual stream at this level of granularity will allow more precise predictions of how
damage to different parts of the brain might affect behavior, and therefore open avenues for the development of
novel diagnostic tools for localizing the locus of a lesion neurologically.

title: Development of Knockin Mouse Models for Study of a Novel Alpha-Synuclein Phosphorylation Site
text:
We seek to understand the relevance of a novel phosphorylation site on α-synuclein, both in a physiological
context and in synucleinopathies such as Multiple Systems Atrophy (MSA). To achieve this, we will develop
and validate a phospho-null T81A α-synuclein knock-in mouse and a phospho-mimetic T81E α-synuclein
knock-in mouse.

title: Autophagy and LC3-associated phagocytosis in intestinal epithelial cells
text:
Specialized membrane trafficking protects the intestinal epithelium from bacteria and viruses, as well as
promotes barrier function of the intestine. However, our understanding of the machinery that regulates these
processes is incomplete. Understanding these processes will provide insight into intestinal disease.

title: Environmental Health Informatics Core
text: ENVIRONMENTAL HEALTH INFORMATICS CORE (EHIC): ABSTRACT The Environmental Health Informatics Core (EHIC) supports CEET investigators using diverse expertise in environmental health informatics, a mission consistent with the existing NIEHS Strategic Plan “To Promote Translation from Data to Knowledge to Action” and that embraces the new area of NIEHS scientific focus in computational biology and data science. Our vision is to provide agile support to CEET investigators on the use of both routine and innovative computational methods to gain insights from large and complex environmental health datasets. In addition, we develop novel analytical strategies when existing approaches are not adequate, and we create efficient workflows to maximize the number of investigators we are able to help. Environmental health scientists are faced with an avalanche of big data unique to this discipline. Unlike other disciplines which may generate traditional “omics” data there is an urgent need to analyze exposomics data (satellite, biosensor, wearable and biomarker data), and relate these data to Electronic Health Records (EHRs), use chemoinformatics to predict the toxicity of unknowns, and extract public health information for epidemiologic studies. We provide bioinformatics, biomedical informatics, chemoinformatics and public health informatics services to accelerate research in these areas. Our bioinformatics services include analysis of many types of omics data, including genomic, transcriptomic, epigenomic, proteomic, lipidomic and metabolomic, as well as their integration using multiomics methods. Our biomedical informatics services include extraction and analysis of data from EHRs, biobanks, and disease registries; digital phenotyping; and use of ontologies to improve interoperability of datasets and their use in large scale research efforts. Our chemoinformatics services include development and use of a graph-knowledge database called ComptoxAI that provides insights into predictive toxicology, adverse outcome pathways, and quantitative structure-activity relationships. Our public health informatics services include analysis of geospatially distributed environmental data, and data collected with pollution sensors, biosensors, and wearable devices. Our services are underpinned by analytical tools that include data science, machine learning, and artificial intelligence. We work closely with the Translational Research Support Core (TRSC) and Biomolecular Mass Spectrometry Core (BMSC) to provide support to the four CEET thematic areas and the crosscutting themes of exposomics and the effects of extreme weather on health.

title: α9α10 Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptors in neuropathic pain
text:
Current medications for the treatment of neuropathic pain are only marginally effective and suffer
from serious, sometimes life-threatening, side effects. Inhibiting the activity of the α9α10 nicotinic
acetylcholine receptor is emerging as a promising strategy to treat neuropathic pain; however,
technical challenges have limited the investigation of this receptor and prevented the discovery
of drugs that target it. This project overcomes this historical hurdle in α9α10 drug discovery to
identify novel α9α10 antagonists and provide strong evidence to support their future development
into new treatments for neuropathic pain.
